newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Oct 28.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Oct 28.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

An historic deal between the Federal Government and the Australian Democrats will see sweeping changes to Australia industrial relations laws come into effect from next February. The deal preserves the central elements of the Government's original legislation, but will allow greater scope for non-union enterprise agreements, drop the existing unfair dismissal laws, and open the way for enterprise unions. Page 1.

The Victorian Director of Public Prosecutions has asked the state's Court of Appeal to rule on 12 questions of law after the acquittal of businessman John Elliott and former Elders IXL executives Peter Scanlon and Ken Biggins - who were all acquitted of fraud and theft charges. Page 3.

Opposition industrial relations spokesman Bob McMullan said yesterday Australian workers would still be worse off under the Workplace Relations Bill, despite changes to the agreement - which was signed by the Democrats and Industrial Relations Minister Peer Reith - secured by the Democrats. Page 4.

Employer, union and welfare groups yesterday gave qualified support to the compromise industrial relations package, however ACTU president Jennie George said the deal was a "significant setback" for the Coalition's industrial agenda. Page 5.
THE AUSTRALIAN

In order to have the Workplace Relations Bill passed by the end of the year, the Federal Government has agreed on 171 changes to the original legislation moved by the Australian Democrats. While not setting any employment targets for the new system, Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith said the changes still maintained the "basic integrity" of the reforms promised in the lead up to the March 2 election. Page 1.

On the eve of a historic debate over euthanasia in Federal Parliament, Federal Liberal MP Kevin Andrews, who designed a Private Member's Bill to override the Northern Territory's euthanasia legislation, said the Territory's attempt to limit the euthanasia law came too late. Page 1.

Under a comprehensive review of the Northern Territory Land Rights Act, the Federal Government will consider dropping the Act's controversial Aboriginal veto powers. The move was criticised last night by the powerful Darwin-based Northern Land Council, which called it an assault on the "heart and soul of land rights". Page 3.

An Australian Broadcasting Authority working paper on the Federal Government's proposed sixth television channel has indicated there is strong support for a community service on the channel. The report said that while there had been support for educational, arts or children's programmes, the majority view is that those types of programmes should be included in a community service. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

The Federal Government has agreed to concessions by the Australian Democrats to secure the passing of the Workplace Relations Bill by the end of the year. Under the controversial deal, the Industrial Relations Commission will have wider powers to regulate wages and conditions and to veto non-union contracts. Page 1.

Around 63,000 New South Wales Year 12 students will today sit the first exam of the Higher School Certificate. As the students prepare for the English exam, the only compulsory subject, parents and teachers have voiced their concerns over the major changes to the controversial scaling system, which will alter the results for thousands of students. Page 1.

New South Wales Opposition Leader Peter Collins has embarrassed Prime Minister John Howard by saying that all political leaders should publicly reject her views. The call comes as an opinion poll, to be published in the Bulletin, shows that if Hanson was to form her own political party, it could win up to 12 seats in the Senate. Page 1.

Federal Liberal MP Kevin Andrews, whose private member's bill is aimed at overturning the Northern Territory's euthanasia laws, has rejected a possible compromise which would see terminally ill people from outside the Territory unable to use its provision. Page 3.
THE AGE

In order to make way for radical changes to Australia's industrial relations laws, the Federal Government has had to make significant concessions to win the support of the Australian Democrats. Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith and Democrats Leader Cheryl Kernot said that after talks lasting 50 hours, the Workplace Relations Bill should be in effect by February next year. Page A1.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett put himself into the role of mediator in a dispute between Sky and Tabcorp that left the screens of the State's 284 TABs blacked out. Kennett was able to extract an A$600,000 concession from Sky Channel's James Packer and also persuaded Packer to change the terms of the contract for the supply of racing footage to TAB agencies. Page A1.

As Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett denies there is any conflict of interest within his Government, his claim will come under scrutiny in Parliament this week, with Attorney-General Jan Wade and Solicitor-General Douglas Graham, QC, under fire for their interests in BHP and Kennett himself being accused of holding shares in Mayne Nickless, one of the three companies awarded a contract to introduce automatic ticketing on public transport. Page A1.

On the eve of the euthanasia debate in the House of Representatives today, Prime Minister John Howard said yesterday the Northern Territory's last-minute offer to limit its world-first euthanasia laws to Territory residents was unlikely to influence voting on the Federal Andrews anti-euthanasia Bill. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
